Exclusive Original Federal Jurisdiction under Article 131 for disputes between the Union and States or between States
Appellate Jurisdiction in constitutional, civil, and criminal matters (Articles 132–134) and Special Leave to Appeal (Article 136)
Power to do 'complete justice' in any cause or matter under Article 142; law declared by SC is binding on all courts in India (Article 141)
Advisory Jurisdiction on questions of law/fact referred by the President (Article 143) and Judicial Review of legislative/executive actions (Articles 13, 32)

nodes.title: Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) & State PSCs
nodes.summary: Independent constitutional recruiting agency safeguarding the merit system in India's civil services by conducting examinations for All-India Services and Central Services (Article 320) and advising on disciplinary and service matters.

nodes.title: Vice-President of India
nodes.summary: Second highest constitutional office in India; acts as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and discharges the functions of the President during casual vacancies (Article 65).

nodes.title: In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution (2023)
nodes.summary: Unanimously upheld the constitutional validity of Presidential Order C.O. 273 of 6 August 2019 declaring that all provisions of the Constitution of India apply to Jammu and Kashmir, holding that Article 370 was a temporary and transitional provision designed for gradual constitutional integration under Article 1.

nodes.title: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)
nodes.summary: Background: Arbitrary dismissal of elected State Governments using President's Rule under Article 356. Holding: Federalism and Secularism are integral parts of the Basic Structure. The President's proclamation under Article 356 is not immune from judicial review; courts can examine whether the proclamation was based on relevant material or mala fide. Whether a Chief Minister enjoys a majority must be tested исключительно on the floor of the Vidhan Sabha (Floor Test), not in the Governor's subjective chamber.

nodes.title: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (Ninth Schedule Case, 2007)
nodes.summary: Unanimously held that any law placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment) is not immune from judicial scrutiny if it damages or destroys the Basic Structure as reflected in the Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21.

nodes.title: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
nodes.summary: Established mandatory nationwide procedural safeguards (arrest memo, informing family/friend, medical inspection, access to lawyer) against custodial torture and arbitrary arrest, later codified into criminal procedure statute.

nodes.title: I.C. Golaknath v. State of Punjab (1967)
nodes.summary: Held by a 6:5 majority (applying prospective overruling) that a Constitutional Amendment is 'law' within the meaning of Article 13(2) and therefore Parliament could not abridge or take away Fundamental Rights—prompting the enactment of the 24th Amendment (1971) and setting the stage for Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

nodes.title: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950)
nodes.summary: The Supreme Court's first major constitutional decision on preventive detention. The majority adopted a positivist, compartmentalized reading of Fundamental Rights (holding that Article 21 only required a procedure enacted by a valid statute, not natural justice or Article 19 reasonableness), while Justice Fazl Ali's famous dissent foreshadowed the integrated Golden Triangle adopted 28 years later in Maneka Gandhi (1978).

nodes.title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (Mandal Commission Case, 1992)
nodes.summary: Upheld 27% reservation for Socially and Educationally Backward Classes (OBCs) in central government employment under Article 16(4); established the 'Creamy Layer' exclusion rule so benefits reach the truly needy, and articulated the general 50% ceiling rule on vertical reservations to balance formal and substantive equality.

nodes.title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
nodes.summary: Heard by the largest bench in Supreme Court history (13 Judges) for 68 days. Background: Challenge to Kerala Land Reforms Acts and the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments. Core Constitutional Question: Is Parliament's power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 unlimited? Holding (7:6 majority): Overruled Golaknath (1967) to hold that Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution including Fundamental Rights, BUT established the Basic Structure Doctrine—Parliament cannot use Article 368 to alter or destroy the basic structure or essential features of the Constitution. Also declared the Preamble an integral part of the Constitution.

nodes.title: Kihoto Hollohon v. Zachilhu (Anti-Defection Case, 1992)
nodes.summary: Upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) while striking down Paragraph 7 (which had barred judicial review), holding that the Speaker acts as a tribunal when deciding disqualification petitions and the Speaker's final decision is subject to judicial review under Articles 136, 226, and 227.

nodes.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
nodes.summary: Background: Impounding of petitioner's passport under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 without giving a pre-decisional hearing or reasons. Core Constitutional Question: Does 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 mean any arbitrary statutory procedure (as held in A.K. Gopalan, 1950)? Holding: Overruled Gopalan's silo theory; established the Golden Triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21. Held that 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be 'right and just and fair, and not arbitrary, fanciful or oppressive', Infusing substantive due process and natural justice into Article 21.

nodes.title: Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980)
nodes.summary: Background: Challenge to Sections 4 and 55 of the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, which gave blanket primacy to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19 and declared that no constitutional amendment could be questioned in any court. Holding: Struck down both provisions as unconstitutional violations of the Basic Structure. Held that limited amending power and judicial review are themselves essential features of the Basic Structure, and that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is a bedrock feature of the Constitution.

nodes.title: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018)
nodes.summary: Unanimously read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code to decriminalize consensual adult same-sex relations, grounding its holding in Constitutional Morality, Transformative Constitutionalism, human dignity, privacy (Puttaswamy), and non-discrimination under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21.

nodes.title: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Assn. v. Union of India (NJAC Case, 2015)
nodes.summary: Struck down the 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act, 2014 by a 4:1 majority, holding that judicial primacy in the appointment of constitutional judges is essential to the independence of the judiciary, which is an unamendable facet of the Basic Structure.

nodes.title: Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985)
nodes.summary: Reading Article 21 in light of Directive Principles (Articles 39(a) and 41), held that the Right to Life includes the Right to Livelihood ('no person can live without the means of living, that is, the means of livelihood') and required fair notice and hearing before eviction of pavement and slum dwellers.

nodes.title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017)
nodes.summary: Background: Reference arising out of challenges to the biometric Aadhaar scheme when the Union argued (citing M.P. Sharma 1954 and Kharak Singh 1962) that the Constitution does not guarantee a fundamental right to privacy. Holding (Unanimous 9:0): Overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh; declared that the Right to Privacy is an inalienable natural right and an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III, grounded in human dignity and individual autonomy. Established the Proportionality Test for evaluating state surveillance, biometric systems, and data protection.

Sharma 1954 and Kharak Singh 1962) that the Constitution does not guarantee a fundamental right to privacy. Holding (Unanimous 9:0): Overruled M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh; declared that the Right to Privacy is an inalienable natural right and an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and Part III, grounded in human dignity and individual autonomy. Established the Proportionality Test for evaluating state surveillance, biometric systems, and data protection.

nodes.title: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
nodes.summary: Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 in its entirety as an unconstitutional, vague, and overbroad restriction on the freedom of speech and expression online under Article 19(1)(a), distinguishing 'discussion' and 'advocacy' from actual 'incitement' to imminent lawless action.

nodes.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
nodes.summary: Held that workplace sexual harassment violates a woman's fundamental rights to gender equality (Articles 14, 15), right to practice any profession (Article 19(1)(g)), and right to life with dignity (Article 21). Invoking Articles 32 and 141 alongside CEDAW and Article 51(c), laid down binding Vishaka Guidelines until Parliament enacted the POSH Act, 2013.

nodes.title: Constitutional Morality
nodes.summary: Introduced into Indian constitutional discourse by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (adapting George Grote): a paramount reverence for the forms and spirit of the Constitution, self-restraint by institutions, and fidelity to pluralistic constitutional values even when they conflict with majoritarian or popular social morality (applied in Naz Foundation, Sabarimala, and Navtej Singh Johar, 2018).

nodes.title: Human Dignity & Individual Autonomy
nodes.summary: The moral cornerstone of Part III and the Preamble. In Maneka Gandhi (1978), Francis Coralie Mullin (1981), and Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), the Supreme Court held that the 'right to life' under Article 21 is not mere animal existence but the right to live with human dignity, encompassing bodily integrity, decisional autonomy, and informational privacy.

nodes.title: Equality (of Status and of Opportunity)
nodes.summary: Combines formal equality ('equality before the law' and 'equal protection of the laws' under Article 14) with substantive and compensatory equality (prohibition of discrimination and affirmative action under Articles 15(4)–(6) and 16(4)–(6), and abolition of untouchability under Article 17).

nodes.title: Cooperative & Asymmetric Federalism
nodes.summary: Described by Granville Austin as 'Cooperative Federalism' and by K.C. Wheare as 'quasi-federal': a constitutional division of sovereignty between the Union and States with a strong unifying framework, intergovernmental cooperation (Finance Commission, GST Council, Inter-State Council), and asymmetric special accommodations (Fifth & Sixth Schedules, Articles 371–371J). Declared part of the Basic Structure in S.R. Bommai (1994).

nodes.title: Fraternity (Assuring the Dignity of the Individual and the Unity and Integrity of the Nation)
nodes.summary: Defined by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as 'a sense of common brotherhood of all Indians—if Indians being one people. It is the principle which gives unity and solidarity to social life.' Uniquely links individual human dignity with national unity and integrity.

nodes.title: Justice (Social, Economic and Political)
nodes.summary: Placed first among the ideals in the Preamble: Social Justice (eliminating caste/gender discrimination and untouchability), Economic Justice (preventing concentration of wealth under Article 39(b)–(c) and ensuring livelihood), and Political Justice (equal voice through universal adult franchise under Article 326).

nodes.title: Liberty (of Thought, Expression, Belief, Faith and Worship)
nodes.summary: Both negative liberty (freedom from arbitrary state restraint under Articles 19–22) and positive liberty (the conditions enabling self-realization and human dignity under Article 21 and Part IV). Dr. B.R. Ambedkar emphasized in his closing speech (25 Nov 1949) that liberty cannot be divorced from equality and fraternity.

nodes.title: Right to Privacy
nodes.summary: Unanimously affirmed by a 9-Judge Constitution Bench in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and across the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. Encompasses bodily integrity, spatial privacy, informational self-determination, and decisional autonomy. Any state infringement (such as surveillance or data collection) must pass the four-prong Proportionality Test: (1) legality (existence of a law), (2) legitimate state aim (e.g., national security), (3) rational nexus & necessity (least restrictive measure), and (4) procedural guarantees against abuse.

nodes.title: Rule of Law
nodes.summary: Supremacy of law over arbitrary power: no person or official is above the law, every executive action must have lawful authority, and independent courts enforce legal limits. Recognized as a core element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution (Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975).

nodes.title: Indian Secularism (Principled Distance & Sarva Dharma Sambhava)
nodes.summary: Unlike strict Western church-state separation, Indian constitutional secularism combines equal freedom of conscience and religion for all (Article 25) and non-establishment (no state religion or religious tax under Article 27) with 'principled distance' that allows the State to reform social evils within religion (Article 25(2)(b)). Declared part of the Basic Structure in S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994).

nodes.title: Separation of Powers & Checks and Balances
nodes.summary: Functional differentiation with institutional checks and balances rather than rigid water-tight separation: the Executive is drawn from and accountable to the Legislature (Article 75(3)), the Judiciary is strictly separated from the Executive (Article 50) and insulated from parliamentary discussion of judicial conduct (Article 121), while exercising judicial review over both.

nodes.title: The Preamble to the Constitution of India
nodes.summary: The solemn philosophical charter of the Constitution declaring the source of authority ('We, the People of India'), the nature of the Indian State (Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic), and its four supreme objectives (Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity).

nodes.title: Constitutional Amendment Process (Article 368)
nodes.summary: Initiated by introducing a Bill in either House of Parliament (never in a State Legislature; does not require prior Presidential recommendation). Must be passed in EACH House separately (no Joint Sitting allowed) by a Special Majority: a majority of the total membership of that House AND a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members of that House present and voting. If the amendment seeks to change federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2) (e.g., Presidential election Art. 54–55, Union/State executive & judiciary, Seventh Schedule, representation of States, or Art. 368 itself), it must ALSO be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States before being presented to the President, who MUST give assent (`shall give his assent`, per 24th Amendment). Subject to Basic Structure review.

nodes.title: Emergency Provisions (National, State/President's Rule, Financial)
nodes.summary: Three constitutional emergency regimes converting the federal system into a unitary structure during crises: (1) National Emergency (Article 352) on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion (requires written Union Cabinet decision and special majority approval by both Houses within 1 month; Articles 20 & 21 can never be suspended per Article 359); (2) Failure of Constitutional Machinery in States / President's Rule (Article 356, subject to judicial review and floor test under S.R. Bommai); and (3) Financial Emergency (Article 360, never invoked in India's history).

nodes.title: General Elections, Formation of Government & Collective Responsibility
nodes.summary: Citizens aged 18+ vote under Universal Adult Suffrage (Article 326) in elections conducted by the Election Commission of India (Article 324) -> 543 MPs elected to Lok Sabha (Article 81) -> President appoints the leader commanding majority support (272+ seats) as Prime Minister (Article 75(1)) -> PM advises appointment of Council of Ministers -> Government proves majority via Vote of Confidence / Floor Test -> Council of Ministers remains in office so long as it retains the confidence of the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3); removable by No-Confidence Motion).

nodes.basis: Articles 74, 75, 81, 85, 324, 326 & Representation of the People Act, 1951

nodes.title: Judicial Review & Writ Jurisdiction (Articles 13, 32, 226)
nodes.summary: Constitutional mechanism by which the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive/administrative orders against: (1) Fundamental Rights under Article 13(2), (2) Federal legislative competence under Articles 245–246, and (3) the Basic Structure Doctrine (for Constitutional Amendments). Enforced via the five prerogative writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, and Certiorari.

nodes.title: Money Bill Procedure & Union Budget (Annual Financial Statement)
nodes.summary: Defined strictly in Article 110(1) (taxation, Consolidated Fund borrowing/appropriation) and certified by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha under Article 110(3). Can be introduced ONLY in the Lok Sabha and ONLY on the recommendation of the President (Article 109(1), 117(1)). Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject a Money Bill; it must return it within 14 days with or without recommendations, which Lok Sabha may accept or reject (Article 109(2)). No Joint Sitting is permissible.

nodes.title: How an Ordinary Bill Becomes an Act of Parliament
nodes.summary: May originate in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (Article 107(1)) -> First Reading (Introduction & Gazette publication) -> Reference to Departmentally Related Standing Committee -> Second Reading (General discussion & clause-by-clause voting) -> Third Reading (Passing) -> Transmission to Second House -> Joint Sitting under Article 108 in case of deadlock -> Presidential Assent under Article 111 (Assent, Withhold, or Return via Suspensive Veto) -> Gazette Notification -> Subordinate Rules & Administrative Enforcement.

nodes.title: Representation of the People Acts, 1950 & 1951
nodes.summary: While Part XV (Articles 324–329) establishes the constitutional skeleton of elections, Parliament enacted the Representation of the People Act, 1950 (allocation of seats, delimitation, voter registration, and electoral rolls) and the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (qualifications and statutory disqualifications of MPs/MLAs, registration of political parties under Section 29A, conduct of elections, corrupt practices, and election petitions before High Courts).

nodes.title: Tenth Schedule — Provisions as to Disqualification on Ground of Defection (Anti-Defection Law)
nodes.summary: Added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 (and strengthened by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 removing the 1/3rd split exception). Disqualifies legislators who voluntarily give up party membership or vote/abstain contrary to party whip, adjudicated by the Speaker/Chairman (subject to judicial review per Kihoto Hollohon, 1992).
nodes.text:
1[TENTH SCHEDULE
[Articles 102(2) and 191(2)]
Provisions as to disqualification on ground of defection
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise requires,—
(a) "House" means either House of Parliament or the Legislative
Assembly or, as the case may be, either House of the Legislature of a State;
(b) "legislature party", in relation to a member of a House
belonging to any political party in accordance with the provisions of
paragraph 2 or 2*** paragraph 4, means the group consisting of all the
members of that House for the time being belonging to that political party
in accordance with the said provisions;
(c) "original political party", in relation to a member of a House,
means the political party to which he belongs for the purposes of sub-
paragraph (1) of paragraph 2;
(d) "paragraph" means a paragraph of this Schedule.
2. Disqualification on ground of defection.—(1) Subject to the
provisions of 3[paragraphs 4 and 5], a member of a House belonging to any
political party shall be disqualified for being a member of the House—
(a) if he has voluntarily given up his membership of such political
party; or
(b) if he votes or abstains from voting in such House contrary to
any direction issued by the political party to which he belongs or by any
person or authority authorised by it in this behalf, without obtaining, in
either case, the prior permission of such political party, person or authority
and such voting or abstention has not been condoned by such political
party, person or authority within fifteen days from the date of such voting
or abstention.
Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-paragraph,—
(a) an elected member of a House shall be deemed to belong to the
political party, if any, by which he was set up as a candidate for election
as such member;
(b) a nominated member of a House shall,—
1. Tenth Schedule added by the Constitution (Fifty-second Amendment) Act, 1985, s. 6
(w.e.f. 1-3-1985).
2. Certain words omitted by the Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Act, 2003, s. 5
(w.e.f. 1-1-2004).
3. Subs. by s. 5, ibid., for "paragraphs 3, 4 and 5" (w.e.f. 1-1-2004).
(i) where he is a member of any political party on the date of
his nomination as such member, be deemed to belong to such
political party;
(ii) in any other case, be deemed to belong to the political
party of which he becomes, or, as the case may be, first becomes,
a member before the expiry of six months from the date on which
he takes his seat after complying with the requirements of article 99
or, as the case may be, article 188.
(2) An elected member of a House who has been elected as such otherwise
than as a candidate set up by any political party shall be disqualified for being a
member of the House if he joins any political party after such election.
(3) A nominated member of a House shall be disqualified for being a
member of the House if he joins any political party after the expiry of six months
from the date on which he takes his seat after complying with the requirements
of article 99 or, as the case may be, article 188.
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of
this paragraph, a person who, on the commencement of the Constitution (Fifty-
second Amendment) Act, 1985, is a member of a House (whether elected or
nominated as such) shall,—
(i) where he was a member of political party immediately before
such commencement, be deemed, for the purposes of sub-paragraph (1) of
this paragraph, to have been elected as a member of such House as a
candidate set up by such political party;
(ii) in any other case, be deemed to be an elected member of the
House who has been elected as such otherwise than as a candidate set up
by any political party for the purposes of sub-paragraph (2) of this
paragraph or, as the case may be, be deemed to be a nominated member
of the House for the purposes of sub-paragraph (3) of this paragraph.

nodes.title: Third Schedule — Forms of Oaths or Affirmations
nodes.summary: Prescribes the constitutional Oaths of Office and Secrecy for Union and State Ministers, candidates and members of Parliament and State Legislatures, Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the CAG.
nodes.text:
THIRD SCHEDULE
[Articles 75(4), 99, 124(6), 148(2), 164(3), 188 and 219]
Forms of Oaths or Affirmations
I
Form of oath of office for a Minister for the Union:—
“I, A. B., do swear in the name of God that I will bear true faith
solemnly affirm
and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established, 1[that I
will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India,] that I will faithfully
and conscientiously discharge my duties as a Minister for the Union and
that I will do right to all manner of people in accordance with the
Constitution and the law, without fear or favour, affection or ill-will.”
II
Form of oath of secrecy for a Minister for the Union:—
“I, A.B., do swear in the name of God that I will not directly or
solemnly affirm
indirectly communicate or reveal to any person or persons any matter
which shall be brought under my consideration or shall become known to
me as a Minister for the Union except as may be required for the due
discharge of my duties as such Minister.”
2[III
A
Form of oath or affirmation to be made by a candidate for election to
Parliament:—
 See also arts. 84 (a) and 173 (a).
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, s. 5 (w.e.f. 5-10-1963).
2. Subs. by s. 5, ibid., for Form III. (w.e.f. 5-10-1963).
“I, A.B., having been nominated as a candidate to fill a seat in the
Council of States (or the House of the People) do swear in the name of God
solemnly affirm
that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by
law established and that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of
India.”
B
Form of oath or affirmation to be made by a member of Parliament:—
“I, A.B., having been elected (or nominated) a member of the
Council of States (or the House of the People) do swear in the name of God
solemnly affirm
that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by
law established, that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India
and that I will faithfully discharge the duty upon which I am about to
enter.”]
IV
Form of oath or affirmation to be made by the Judges of the Supreme
Court and the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India:—
“I, A.B., having been appointed Chief Justice (or a Judge) of the
Supreme Court of India (or Comptroller and Auditor-General of
India) do swear in the name of God that I will bear true faith and
solemnly affirm
faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established,
1[that I will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India,] that I will duly
and faithfully and to the best of my ability, knowledge and judgment
perform the duties of my office without fear or favour, affection or ill-will
and that I will uphold the Constitution and the laws.”
1. Ins. by the Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act, 1963, s. 5 (w.e.f. 5-10-1963).

“I, A.B., do swear in the name of God that I will bear true faith

and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established, 1[that I
will uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India,] that I will faithfully

. and that I will do right to all manner of people in accordance with

nodes.title: Fourth Schedule — Allocation of Seats in the Council of States (Rajya Sabha)

nodes.title: Fifth Schedule — Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes
nodes.summary: Establishes Tribes Advisory Councils and empowers the Governor to direct whether or with what modifications Union/State laws apply to Scheduled Areas and to make regulations for peace and good government (protective land transfer restrictions).
nodes.text:
FIFTH SCHEDULE
[Article 244(1)]
Provisions as to the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and
Scheduled Tribes
PART A
GENERAL
1. Interpretation.—In this Schedule, unless the context otherwise
requires, the expression “State” 1*** does not include the 2[States of Assam
3[, 4[Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.]]]
2. Executive power of a State in Scheduled Areas.—Subject to the
provisions of this Schedule, the executive power of a State extends to the
Scheduled Areas therein.
3. Report by the Governor 5*** to the President regarding the
administration of Scheduled Areas.—The Governor 5*** of each State having
Scheduled Areas therein shall annually, or whenever so required by the President,
make a report to the President regarding the administration of the Scheduled
Areas in that State and the executive power of the Union shall extend to the
giving of directions to the State as to the administration of the said areas.
PART B
ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL OF SCHEDULED AREAS AND
SCHEDULED TRIBES
4. Tribes Advisory Council.—(1) There shall be established in each
State having Scheduled Areas therein and, if the President so directs, also in any
State having Scheduled Tribes but not Scheduled Areas therein, a Tribes
Advisory Council consisting of not more than twenty members of whom, as
nearly as may be, three-fourths shall be the representatives of the Scheduled
Tribes in the Legislative Assembly of the State:
1. The words and letters "means a State specified in Part A or Part B of the First Schedule
but" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f.
1-11-1956).
2. Subs. by the North-Eastern Areas (Reorganisation) Act, 1971 (81 of 1971), s. 71, for
"State of Assam" (w.e.f. 21-1-1972).
3. Subs. by the Constitution (Forty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1984, s. 3, for "and
Meghalaya" (w.e.f. 1-4-1985).
4. Subs. by the State of Mizoram Act, 1986 (34 of 1986), s. 39, for "Meghalaya and
Tripura" (w.e.f. 20-2-1987).
5. The words "or Rajpramukh" omitted by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act,
1956, s. 29 and Sch. (w.e.f. 1-11-1956).
Provided that if the number of representatives of the Scheduled Tribes in
the Legislative Assembly of the State is less than the number of seats in the Tribes
Advisory Council to be filled by such representatives, the remaining seats shall
be filled by other members of those tribes.
(2) It shall be the duty of the Tribes Advisory Council to advise on such
matters pertaining to the welfare and advancement of the Scheduled Tribes in the
State as may be referred to them by the Governor 1***.
(3) The Governor 2*** may make rules prescribing or regulating, as the
case may be,—
(a) the number of members of the Council, the mode of their
appointment and the appointment of the Chairman of the Council and of
the officers and servants thereof;
(b) the conduct of its meetings and its procedure in general; and
(c) all other incidental matters.
5. Law applicable to Scheduled Areas.—(1) Notwithstanding anything
in this Constitution, the Governor 1*** may by public notification direct that any
particular Act of Parliament or of the Legislature of the State shall not apply to
a Scheduled Area or any part thereof in the State or shall apply to a Scheduled
Area or any part thereof in the State subject to such exceptions and modifications
as he may specify in the notification and any direction given under this sub-
paragraph may be given so as to have retrospective effect.
(2) The Governor may make regulations for the peace and good
government of any area in a State which is for the time being a Scheduled Area.
In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing
power, such regulations may—
(a) prohibit or restrict the transfer of land by or among members of
the Scheduled Tribes in such area;

nodes.title: Sixth Schedule — Provisions as to the Administration of Tribal Areas in the States of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
nodes.summary: Establishes Autonomous Districts and Autonomous Regions with elected District Councils and Regional Councils possessing legislative, judicial, land, forest, and taxation powers.

nodes.title: Seventh Schedule — List I (Union List), List II (State List), List III (Concurrent List)
nodes.summary: The core legislative division of powers in India's federation: List I — Union List (p. 341–347: Defence, Atomic Energy, Foreign Affairs, Railways, Banking, Currency, Corporation Tax, Inter-State Trade); List II — State List (p. 348–351: Public Order, Police, Public Health, Agriculture, Land, Local Government, State Public Services); List III — Concurrent List (p. 352–355: Criminal Law & Procedure, Marriage & Divorce, Contracts, Forests, Education, Trade Unions, Electricity).
